findings.title: Unchecked Optional.get() breaks login form for user-storage recovery codes
findings.body: `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` returns an `Optional`, and the result is dereferenced with `.get()` without an `isPresent()` check. With this PR, recovery codes can now be owned by a user-storage provider: `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.configuredFor()` only asks `isConfiguredFor(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE)` (a `CredentialInputValidator` call), while `getCredential()` relies on the provider also exposing the credential through `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`. A provider that validates the credential but does not expose it (a very common combination, e.g. a provider implementing only `CredentialInputValidator`/`CredentialInputUpdater`) will make the authenticator render this bean, and the empty `Optional` throws `NoSuchElementException`, resulting in a 500 error page instead of a login challenge. The same applies to `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get()` on line 21. Both need a graceful fallback/error path.

findings.title: Pre-existing local recovery-codes credential is left valid after codes are stored in user storage
findings.body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential()` calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` and, when the user-storage provider handles it, skips creating/replacing the local credential entirely. Any previously stored *local* recovery-codes credential for that user is neither removed nor overwritten. This is exactly the upgrade scenario this PR targets: a federated user who configured recovery codes before the provider supported the type keeps the old local credential, and `SubjectCredentialManager.isValid()` will still accept those old codes via the local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider`. Re-generating recovery codes must invalidate the previous set; here the old codes stay valid indefinitely. Additionally `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` now prefers the federated credential, so the stale local credential is invisible in the UI while remaining usable for authentication.

findings.title: User label and generation timestamp are dropped when codes are stored in user storage
findings.body: The credential handed to the user-storage provider is built as `new UserCredentialModel("", type, recoveryCodesJson)`, i.e. only the raw codes are transferred; the `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` (which carries the user-entered label from the `userLabel` form field and the `generatedAt` timestamp) is used only on the local-storage branch. Consequently, for federated users the label the user typed in the required-action form is silently discarded and cannot be shown in the account/admin console. The new value format (a JSON array of raw codes in `getChallengeResponse()` on update, versus a single raw code on validation) is also completely undocumented in the method javadoc, so third-party provider authors cannot implement `updateCredential` for this type correctly.

findings.title: Exhausted federated recovery-codes credential is removed from the wrong store
findings.body: `getCredential()` can now return a credential coming from the user-storage provider (via `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`), but when `allCodesUsed()` is true the code still calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`, which only addresses Keycloak's local credential store. For a federated credential this is a no-op (and the id may even be null, since providers typically build the model with `createFromValues(...)` which does not set an id), so the exhausted credential is left in the user storage. Removal/disabling for federated credentials has to go through the provider (`disableCredentialType`), otherwise the stale credential stays reported as configured.

findings.title: getCredentials() dereferences a possibly null MyUser
findings.body: `var myUser = getMyUser(user);` is immediately dereferenced (`myUser.recoveryCodes`) without the null check that every other method in this class performs (`isConfiguredFor`, `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`, `isValid` all handle `null`). `getMyUser()` returns null whenever the username is not in the in-memory map (e.g. a user still cached/linked in Keycloak after being removed from the provider), which turns a credential listing into a NullPointerException propagated to the caller.

findings.title: Recovery codes cannot be disabled/removed although the type is now reported as supported
findings.body: `supportsCredentialType()` (line 114) and `isConfiguredFor()` (line 275) were extended for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE`, but `disableCredentialType()` (line 217) still only handles OTP and `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream()` (line 255) only ever reports `CredentialModel.OTP`. As a result, a recovery-codes credential stored in this provider can never be deleted or disabled through the admin/account REST APIs, and the new tests do not cover removal at all (unlike the OTP flows, which have `testOTPSetupThroughAdminRESTAndLogin` / `testDisableCredentialsInUserStorage`). Since this provider doubles as the reference for user-storage credential support, the gap will be copied by implementors.

findings.title: New test never verifies that a recovery code is consumed/single-use
findings.body: `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` logs in once with code index 0 and asserts the requested code number is 0. Because `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid` (line 340) merely checks membership in the stored list and `getCredentials` (line 237) rebuilds the model with `createFromValues`, which marks all codes unused, every login will accept the very same code forever and the prompt will always ask for code #1. The single-use semantics of recovery codes — the core security property of the feature, and the behaviour `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean`/`allCodesUsed()` depend on — are therefore neither exercised nor supported by the reference provider. At minimum a second login should assert that the previously used code is rejected and/or that the requested code index advances.

findings.title: Login in new test is not completed and logout result is ignored
findings.body: Unlike the sibling OTP test (`testOTPUpdateAndLogin`, which calls `testAppHelper.completeLogin()` before `appPage.assertCurrent()` and wraps logout in `assertTrue(...)`), `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` never calls `completeLogin()` after submitting the recovery code and discards the `testAppHelper.logout()` return value. The code-to-token exchange is thus never performed and a failing logout is silently swallowed, leaving the user session behind and potentially affecting subsequent tests in this class (which all reuse the username "otp1").
